questions.question: In an elliptic-curve group, what acts as the identity element for point addition?
options: The point at infinity (often written 𝒪)
The point (0, 0) on the curve
Any point with x = 0
The point with the smallest x-coordinate
questions.explanation: Elliptic-curve groups include a special identity element called the point at infinity 𝒪. Adding 𝒪 leaves any point unchanged.

questions.question: For distinct affine points P=(x1,y1) and Q=(x2,y2) on a short Weierstrass curve over F_p, what is the slope λ used in addition formulas?
options: λ = x1·x2 + y1·y2 (mod p)
questions.explanation: When P ≠ Q, the group law uses the chord slope λ = (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1) modulo p (i.e., multiply by the modular inverse of x2 − x1).

questions.question: What should point_add return when x1 = x2 and y1 ≡ −y2 (mod p)?
options: The point at infinity 𝒪 (the identity)
A ValueError because the points are invalid
The point (x1, 0) regardless of y1
The midpoint of P and Q in F_p
questions.explanation: If Q = −P, the line through P and Q is vertical. In the group law this case returns the identity 𝒪 (represented as infinity).

questions.question: For point doubling (P = Q), which slope formula is used on a short Weierstrass curve y^2 = x^3 + a·x + b over F_p (p > 3)?
options: λ = (y1 − y2) / (x1 − x2) (mod p) with y2 = y1
questions.explanation: Doubling uses the tangent line at P. Over short Weierstrass curves, the tangent slope is λ = (3x1^2 + a)/(2y1) modulo p.

questions.question: Why does a short Weierstrass curve require a non-zero discriminant condition like 4a^3 + 27b^2 ≠ 0 (mod p)?
options: To ensure the curve is non-singular, so the group law behaves correctly
To ensure every x has exactly one y solution
To ensure scalar multiplication is constant-time automatically
To ensure p is prime
questions.explanation: If the curve is singular, it has cusps/self-intersections and does not form the intended elliptic-curve group. The discriminant condition rules those cases out.

questions.question: In the affine addition formulas over F_p, what does “division” mean?
options: Multiply by a modular inverse in F_p, if it exists
Use floating-point division then round to the nearest integer
Shift right by one bit when p is odd
Subtract the denominator until the numerator is small
questions.explanation: Over F_p, division is multiplication by an inverse: a/b means a·b^{-1} modulo p, and b^{-1} exists only when b ≠ 0 mod p.

questions.question: In an ECDH-style protocol, what is the core risk if you multiply an untrusted small-order point Q by your secret scalar k and expose the result?
options: It can leak k modulo the small order r of Q (a small-subgroup / invalid-curve pattern)
It forces k to be even, making brute force easier
It makes modular inverses stop existing for the correct curve
It lets the attacker compute k exactly in one query for any curve
questions.explanation: If Q has order r, then k·Q only takes r possible values. Observing the output can reveal k mod r, which can be combined across queries to recover more information.

questions.question: Which combination best prevents invalid-point pitfalls in real-world ECC protocols?
options: Validate the point is on the intended curve, and enforce correct subgroup membership where relevant
Only validate that x and y are within [0, p-1]
Skip validation because the formulas will fail safely when the point is invalid
Validate the point, but only after doing scalar multiplication
questions.explanation: Safe ECC implementations validate untrusted points and, depending on the curve/protocol, also ensure they lie in the correct prime-order subgroup (or use cofactor clearing).
